## Where the last session left off

- A thousand people on a grid, contacts drawn from the twenty-four neighbours
  within two cells.
- Everyone behaves the same way from the first day to the last.
- Widening the neighbourhood from eight people to twenty-four changed a single
  introduction from almost never establishing to establishing about half the
  time.

This session adds one thing: people who notice what is happening around them.

::: {.notes}
Recap only as far as is needed to start.  The grid, the two-phase update and
`nearby_agents` all carry over unchanged, so nothing about the API is new today.

The last bullet is the hook.  The previous session showed that *who you meet*
changes the epidemic; this one asks what happens when *what you know* changes
too.
:::

## One rule about behaviour

A susceptible person who can see at least $m$ infectious people within
`info_radius` cells takes precautions for that step:

$$
\beta \longrightarrow \beta(1-\alpha).
$$

Three numbers, each of them a modelling assumption:

- `info_radius`, how far a person's information reaches;
- $m$, how many cases it takes before they act;
- $\alpha$, how much good the precautions do.

::: {.notes}
Note that the information radius and the contact radius are separate numbers.
News travels further than infection: you meet the people next door and you hear
about the street.  Setting them equal would be the claim that everyone knows the
status of exactly the people who could infect them.

Nothing here makes precautions persist.  Somebody who sees no infection this step
behaves normally again, which is worth flagging before anyone asks.
:::

## The same behaviour, three kinds of information

| Setting | What a person can see |
|---|---|
| `:none` | nothing; last session's model |
| `:local` | the infectious people within `info_radius` cells |
| `:national` | reported prevalence $I/N$, acting once it passes $\theta$ |

The precautions are identical in all three. Only the trigger differs.

::: {.notes}
This table is the design of the whole session.  Holding the behaviour fixed and
varying only the information is what isolates the effect, and it is the move that
makes the result about individual-level modelling rather than about how strong an
intervention is.

`:national` is the version a compartmental model can already express, as a
transmission rate that falls with prevalence.  Say that now; Part C returns to it.
:::

## Counting what behaviour costs

Either rule can be made stronger by having more people take precautions for
longer, so comparing outcomes alone proves nothing.

**Aware person-days**: susceptible people taking precautions, times the length
of the step, added up over the epidemic.

```julia
model.aware_days += model.Δt *
    count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model))
```

Match the two rules on that, then compare the epidemics.

::: {.notes}
This is the idea participants are most likely to skip past, so it is worth
stating twice: without a cost measure, "the local rule works better" only means
"this setting of the local rule was stronger than that setting of the national
one".

The measure is crude.  Every person-day counts the same whether it
is a mask or a closed shop, and the model has nothing to say about which.  That
limitation is one of the discussion questions.
:::

Same precautions. Nearly the same behaviour spent. Very different epidemics.

::: {.notes}
Eight seeds, the same set the worksheet uses, so the numbers on this slide are
the ones participants will reproduce.

Do not explain the mechanism yet.  Put the three rows on the screen, ask the room
why two of them differ so much when the precautions are identical, and let the
worksheet be where they find out.  The answer is targeting: local information
spends its precautions on people standing next to a case, and on this grid that
is where all the transmission is.
:::

## Why this needs agents

- The national rule is a function of $I/N$. A compartmental model can carry it
  as $\beta(I)$ and needs no individuals.
- The local rule is a function of *one person's own neighbourhood*.
- Writing it in $S$, $I$ and $R$ would need the number of
  susceptible-infectious neighbour pairs, then triples, and so on. The system
  does not close.

When behaviour depends on what each person can see, an individual-level model
is not a more detailed route to the same answer. It is the only way to ask.

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that justifies the session existing, and it is the one to
protect if time runs short.

Be careful not to oversell.  Pair approximations and moment closures do exist and
are used; the honest statement is that closing the system requires an
approximation whose error is exactly the correlation the rule depends on.
:::

## What the model assumes, and does not {.smaller}

- Anyone close enough to infect you is close enough for you to see: the
  information radius of 3 contains the contact radius of 2. At $m=1$ nobody at
  risk is missed, and that is most of why the local rule does so well.
- People know their neighbours' status at once and for free. In reality
  infection precedes symptoms and reporting takes days, so protection would
  arrive late.
- Every aware person-day costs the same, whether it is a mask or a closed shop.
- Nobody stays careful once their neighbourhood looks clear.

The measured advantage of local information is a ceiling, not a forecast.

::: {.notes}
The first bullet is the mechanism rather than a caveat, so do not hurry it.
Under the Chebyshev metric a ball of radius 3 contains one of radius 2, so any
infectious person who could reach you is inside your information radius, and at
$m=1$ the rule never misses anyone at risk.  It stops holding at $m\ge2$, where
you can have one infectious neighbour and still not act, and the worksheet sweep
prices that: 47 infections at $m=1$ against 140 at $m=2$.

Both information failures in the second bullet push the same way, which is why
the ceiling framing is the right one.

The last bullet is the most inviting thing to change.  Adding a memory to
`is_aware`, so precautions last a few days after the last case seen, is a
two-line edit and a good answer to "what should I try next".
:::

## Takeaways and links

- A space defines a neighbourhood; a neighbourhood defines who you meet and
  what you can see, and those need not be the same set.
- Compare behavioural rules at matched cost, or you are comparing strengths.
- A response too weak to break transmission costs more and achieves less.

::: {.notes}
The third takeaway is the one participants tend to find surprising, and it
generalises past this model: the cost of a behavioural response is paid per
person per unit time, so anything that shortens the epidemic is cheaper than it
looks and anything that merely stretches it is dearer.
:::
